    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Blake Griffin told an interesting story recently, recalling playing golf with former teammate JJ Redick.
    • In a recent development, this was before Redick became the head coach of the Lakers.
    • According to recent reports, "The way I took it and the way I think that he meant it," Griffin told GQ, "is it's such a grind, mental grind, physical grind of putting literally everything you have into this thing.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Blake Griffin told an interesting story recently, recalling playing golf with former teammate JJ Redick. At that point, Redick was already retired and Griffin was nearing the end of his career.

    In a recent development, this was before Redick became the head coach of the Lakers. He had some perspective on his post-playing days that he offered to Griffin, something that stuck with the longtime Clipper years later. Redick told Griffin that he wouldn't be "truly happy" until he retired. Knowing how that might sound, Griffin was quick to clarify that they weren't miserable playing basketball, but rather that the two men were similar in their extensive, obsessive preparation.

    According to recent reports, "The way I took it and the way I think that he meant it," Griffin told GQ, "is it's such a grind, mental grind, physical grind of putting literally everything you have into this thing. And then when you're done, you just find this latest sense of peace.".

    Industry observers note that put another way, pressure is baked into being in the NBA. The severity might vary from player to player or team to team, but it's natural enough to feel a certain amount of weight given the intensity of the competition. With that in mind, here are some estimations on current stress levels around the league.

    According to recent reports, all things considered, the Sixers have to be pretty happy with how they've started the season. Even after the Blazers snapped their five-game win streak on Monday, Philly is 14-4 and sits atop the East. LeBron James, unsurprisingly, has been a fantastic addition, particularly as a distributor and playmaker. Jaylen Brown is playing his usual heavy minutes while shooting nearly 50% from the floor. And, crucially, Joel Embiid — who missed a combined 150 games over the previous three seasons — has appeared in all but four games to date. Those are all wins for the Sixers.

    Recent findings suggest that to the extent that there's any cause for concern here, it's how sustainable all this is for them. Of the 18 games they've played, they're a perfect 12-0 in the clutch (games decided by five points or fewer with five minutes or less to go). That's tops in the NBA, and they must feel good about being at their best when things get a little dicey. But as Tyrese Maxey pointed out earlier in the season when they were starting to fall into this rhythm of playing close game after close game, he and the Sixers would prefer to stack a few victories that don't cause them to sweat right until the end.

    Winning in the clutch sure beats the alternative. For now, it's less of a problem than something to monitor.

    Just a couple of weeks ago, the Celtics won the battle of frenemies and were perched atop the Eastern Conference. Things haven't gone quite to initiative since then. All of a sudden, the Celtics have lost four in a row, including two one-point losses at Sacramento and Golden State. Boston handed the Kings just their second win of the season, and dropped the game to the Stephen Curry-less Warriors. Not the kind of basketball the Celtics are accustomed to playing.

    In a recent development, things haven't been easy lately for Boston. The Sacramento and Golden State games were on a back-to-back as part of a difficult, still-in-progress stretch in the schedule in which Boston plays six of seven on the road, culminating in another back-to-back when the Celtics face the Spurs in San Antonio this coming Sunday, followed by the Mavericks in Dallas on Monday.

    Sources indicate that perhaps most troubling of all, two-way star Derrick White has been merely a one-way contributor for a while now. White had a disappointing shooting season a year ago. Considering his talent, the smart bet was that he would bounce back and be more efficient this season. That hasn't happened. White is shooting 41% from the floor and an abysmal 28.9% from deep. The 3-point mark is the worst of his career by a good stretch. He made just 2 of 12 from distance against the Warriors and was visibly frustrated with himself.

    The Celtics have long had a theory of how they like to play: take and make more 3s than the opposition on any given night. When their shots are falling, they're tough to beat. When they aren't, anyone can knock them off. Right now, they're struggling, White in particular. Boston doesn't really have any choice but to let White try to shoot his way back into form. He's too key to their overall intends, and they'd never be able to replace his impact at the other end of the floor, where he remains one of the best all-around defenders in the league. Either he fixes his shot and Boston is back in business, or he doesn't and life at the office gets a lot tougher for everyone.

    According to recent reports, when the Timberwolves announced in October that Anthony Edwards would undergo an arthroscopic procedure on his right knee, it took some people by surprise. Edwards looked good to start the season. He torched the Heat in the opening outing, going for 45 points and draining nine 3s. In his fourth game, on the second night of a back-to-back, he put up 47 points in a close two-point loss at Cleveland — and then suddenly and without warning, he was out of commission and expected to miss approximately two months.

    Edwards recently said that he "never wanted to have surgery" and he felt pretty good during the offseason. He thought he was managing the knee well then, and it wasn't swollen during the summer. But after the aforementioned back-to-back, the knee "was really bad, like painful to fly. So I'm like, 'I'm gonna get [the surgery].'".

    Sources indicate that without him, the Wolves have fared better than some might have expected, going a tidy 10-4. They're third in the Western Conference, trailing only the Spurs and Lakers. That should have head coach Chris Finch and the Wolves optimistic about staying afloat until Edwards returns. Except no one seems to be sure when that might be, including Edwards, who recently cast some doubt on the initial timetable when he mentioned he has "no clue" when he'll be back on the floor.

    According to recent reports, if we go by the original estimation, two months would put Ant in late December. Now that ballpark appears far less than certain. The Wolves have performed admirably with him sidelined, but in a loaded West, Minnesota will need Edwards back sooner than "no clue" if it wants to stay near the top of the conference and especially if the Wolves hope to make a deep postseason run.

    Industry observers note that ant is the unquestionable leader in all departments for Minnesota. In his absence, things have sometimes felt a little tense  — to the point where one noted knucklehead has periodically gotten frustrated by another. Getting Edwards back would definitely help on the court. It wouldn't hurt the vibes, either.

    In a recent development, what are the Cavs even doing? They're 9-9 after losing to the Bulls (without Caleb Wilson, no less) on Monday. That puts them one game up on the Magic for seventh in the East. They're just 2-6 outside of Cleveland. But hey, James Harden recently went for 51 points against the Pacers and now has more 50-point games in his career than Kobe Bryant. Maybe that will console Cavs fans. Seems unlikely, though.

    It has been revealed that when you reach the conference finals, bring back your four most crucial players and add a fifth starter coming off a promising season, the expectations are understandably high. So far, the Cavs haven't exactly met them. Cleveland has been a top 10 offensive team, but bottom 10 in defense. That leaves them pretty much looking like what their record indicates — average at best, a team that could lose to an inferior opponent (like, say, Chicago) on any random night in November.

    Recent findings suggest that it certainly hasn't helped that they've been without Evan Mobley of late. He's missed the last six games with a toe injury. Peyton Watson, the aforementioned addition to the starting lineup, hasn't been anywhere near as good in Cleveland as he was in Denver last season. All of that has left Donovan Mitchell with too much heavy lifting, and so far he hasn't been able to shoulder the load on his own. The longer this mediocrity continues, the more we're left to wonder whether the Cavs are overdue to shake up their starting unit and offload one of the big names.

    [Looks around to see if anyone else is cringing] They just lost to the Pacers.

    According to recent reports, in fairness, no team has been hit with more major injuries than the Thunder. Jalen Williams (leg) and Cason Wallace (shoulder) could very well miss the remainder of the season after both underwent surgery, while Chet Holmgren (knee) is expected to miss at least three months. That's three of the team's five starters to begin the season. Not good. Except to hear the reigning back-to-back MVP tell it, there's something unexpected to be gleaned from the experience.

    "Honestly speaking, it's kind of fun," Shai Gilgeous-Alexander remarked last week. "We've kind of had the wind at our back the last couple of years and had our way a lot of nights, and to have that kind of adversity, it's kind of fun. I embrace it. It'll make me better.".

    In a recent development, SGA has a different definition of fun than most people. After losing in Indiana on Monday, the Thunder are just two games over .500, which puts them 10th in the West. [Go ahead and cringe if you weren't already doing so.].

    If there's any team that can withstand SGA's bizarre version of a good time, it's the Thunder. Sam Presti assembled the deepest team in the NBA, but there are limits to what even they can handle. In the absence of several key players, Ajay Mitchell, Jared McCain, Isaiah Hartenstein and others have all been tasked with picking up considerable slack. That includes rookies Aday Mara and Bennett Stirtz. When you're missing so many notable pieces, you stop being deep at some point and just do your best to plug holes. Even the mighty Thunder can only do so much.

    The Warriors snapped a five-game losing streak by beating the Celtics at home on Sunday in a white-knuckled one-point win. Alas, they only managed 88 points in the victory and the offense looked super sluggish yet again. Even with the win over Boston, the Warriors are 9-8 and 11th in the West standings. Things have gone sideways when you're looking up at everyone but the Pelicans, Clippers, Jazz and Kings.

    In a recent development, the Warriors' start to the season was fun while it lasted. Yaxel Lendeborg played great — and talked just as well — and immediately cemented himself in the starting lineup, not to mention the Rookie of the Year race. Even more encouraging, Stephen Curry looked like a vintage version of himself again after playing just 43 games a season ago. Through the first 11 games this year, Curry was second in the league in scoring behind only Luka Dončić. He appeared sharp and healthy — until he came out of the game in Houston in early November while holding his side after playing just six minutes. Turned out to be an abdominal tear. The Warriors revealed that he would be reevaluated in two weeks, though the general ballpark for that kind of injury is closer to a month.

    It has been revealed that not great, especially considering the Warriors were hardly at full strength as it was. Jimmy Butler and Moses Moody have yet to play a single minute while both recover from knee injuries. Meanwhile, Kristaps Porziņģis — who signed a new two-year deal worth $40 million in the offseason — is dealing with health challenges and recently stepped away from basketball. Curry is the most critical piece of all, but not having several key components has left the Warriors painfully thin. That has reminded the Warriors how much tougher life is for all of them when Curry isn't on the floor and a rookie is suddenly tasked with leading the way.

    The recently ended losing streak included a stretch at San Antonio, Latest Orleans, Dallas and Memphis during which the average margin of defeat was more than 27 points. The loss to the Spurs was bad enough that Lendeborg came back with a new cut, prompting Steve Kerr to quip that the rookie dealt with the defeat by "[chopping] all his hair off.".

    Through it all, Draymond hasn't been able to stop being Draymond. Green spent the run-up to the Celtics meeting warring with an NBA unc online, then got called for a tech while sitting on the bench during the game. Take a breath and go for a walk, man.

    Sources indicate that curry can't return soon enough. If this goes on much longer, Yaxel and the rest of them will be fully bald.

    #119086. Barbra Banda talks a 2021 in which she rose to global prominence and the future

    📅 23 Jan 2022 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2024 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thesefootballtimes ↗ Open Full Page

    Barbra Banda talks a 2021 in which she rose to global prominence and the future

    📅 23 Jan 2022 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2024 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thesefootballtimes

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, very few footballers anywhere in the world shot to prominence in 2021 quite like Zambia forward Barbra Banda.
    • It was the very first appearance for the Copper Queens at a women’s football tournament, and ranked outside the world’s top 100, few gave them a chance of competing in a group that included China, Brazil and European champions, the Netherlands.
    • A 10-3 defeat in their opening game against the latter emphasised the gap, but was memorable for the 21-year-old scoring an extraordinary hat-trick, with two or her goals coming in the space of a minute towards the end of the game with the result already beyond doubt.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, very few footballers anywhere in the world shot to prominence in 2021 quite like Zambia forward Barbra Banda. A name familiar to those who follow the women’s game in-depth, but perhaps an unknown to many, Banda changed that in the space of four incredible days during the summer Olympic Games in Tokyo.

    It was the very first appearance for the Copper Queens at a women’s football tournament, and ranked outside the world’s top 100, few gave them a chance of competing in a group that included China, Brazil and European champions, the Netherlands.

    A 10-3 defeat in their opening game against the latter emphasised the gap, but was memorable for the 21-year-old scoring an extraordinary hat-trick, with two or her goals coming in the space of a minute towards the end of the game with the result already beyond doubt.

    As if that wasn’t enough, Banda hit another hat-trick just three days later in a thrilling 4-4 draw against China, becoming the first player ever to score back-to-back Olympic hat-tricks.

    Sitting in her hotel room in China where she is undergoing mandatory isolation after returning from a national team camp, Banda reflects on a period that propelled into the eyes of the world on the biggest stage available. “I never thought I would represent Zambia on that kind of stage,” she says. “I always told myself it’s about hard work and determination that gets you there and then suddenly I found myself representing my country at an Olympics.”.

    Throughout our interview, Banda is humble, but more than anything continuously emphasises how her whole career has, and will continue to be, about hard work, about determination, that she hasn’t yet come close to achieving what she wants, even reflecting that the tournament was somewhat of a disappointment despite what they were up against and the personal history she made.

    “We didn’t do our level best to go to the second round, but for our team just being there was a great achievement, for our country, for Africa, because we were the only African team there. It was history for us just to qualify for Tokyo. The achievement of scoring those two hat-tricks, it’s just the result of what kind of person I am. I work hard, I am always there for my team and for my country and all I do is aim to do the best for my country.”.

    Despite only turning 21 this year and having a large part of her career still in front of her, it has been a long and eventful journey for Banda just to get to where she is now, growing up in a country where women’s football was far from prominent.

    Banda joined an academy as a youngster and spent over 10 years there, and it was the motivation she got from her dad in particular which inspired her to continue following her dream. “For me, I started very early, I just used to go and play football with my dad. At the academy, that’s when I started playing competitively in a league for women in Zambia.

    “Things happened quite quickly. At the age of 13 I was called up for trials for the under 17 national team and ended up doing to play in Costa Rica at the under 17 World Cup in Costa Rica.”.

    Yes, at the age of just 13, Banda was representing her nation at a major FIFA tournament, where she was incredibly only the second-youngest player behind 12-year-old Ghanaian defender Fuseina Mumuni; a tournament that saw Banda suddenly gracing the same pitches as other promising youngsters such as Deyna Castellanos, Lea Schüller, Jessie Fleming, Patri Guijarro and Aitana Bonmatí.

    In a recent development, “After that I moved clubs, went to a bigger club, the Green Buffalos in Zambia. I think that’s when I started with the senior national team and started to become a bit more well-known to people.

    According to recent reports, “As time went on I was still so inspired by my dad,” she recalls. “He was always there for me in terms of football. It’s interesting because it was really only him who was interested, my mum didn’t want me to play football. I wanted to play and my dad encouraged me, but my mum wanted me to go to school and get an education. But, now they’re both happy with how I’m doing.”.

    By this time Banda was starting to gain attention from around the world as she looked to take the next step in her career, and found an agent, Anton, who is on the call too, with the pair now having worked together for several years and formed a close working relationship.

    Several Spanish clubs in particular were interested in signing Banda in the summer of 2018 but weren’t overly convinced about taking who was then a relatively unknown African striker who hadn’t played football outside Zambia.

    There was also the issue of the looming annual COSAFA Cup in Africa, which would take place in September at the very start of the European season, with several interested clubs demanding Banda miss the tournament. One of those who passed up the opportunity was relegated at the end of the season.

    Industry observers note that in the end, newly-promoted Logroño took the chance on Banda and the teenager went on to score 16 goals in 28 league appearances for the club across a two-year stay in Spain. “That was a great move or me and I always thank Anton, he has always been there for me,” she smiles. “He knows what it takes to have a player and put trust in that player when nobody else believes in you. He believed in me and made it possible for me to move to Spain.

    Sources indicate that “Many clubs wouldn’t accept African players, they didn’t think we were at that level, but I went there and revealed in Africa that we do have good players. Everyone there was happy with me. The players, the management, everyone was happy. I enjoyed Spain, it was competitive, they love football there and every game was very hard and very strong.”.

    It was not just a big move for Banda on the pitch, but off it. It meant a first move away not just from Zambia, but Africa. At the age of 18, Banda was leaving behind everything and everyone she’d ever known in the search of making football a career for her and to show other young girls in Zambia it could be done.

    Industry observers note that “Being the first time, my parents were a bit worried, but I think there was a good side as well because they’d got used to me going away for weeks and months with the national team. I think that contributed to them understanding, they had to accept it.”.

    It wasn’t just her family Banda had to convince either. Extraordinarily, Banda was undergoing mandatory military service in Zambia at the time and had to get permission from the colonel of the Zambian army which she laughs “wasn’t easy” when discussing the story.

    Recent findings suggest that “It was so difficult! That’s why I really appreciate Anton, because he worked so hard for me. I was coming from military service, there was a lot of paperwork, a lot of explanations, so it wasn’t easy. The Zambian army commander is now the women’s representative for women’s football in Zambia. She did a lot of good work for me to get permission from the colonel of the army which meant I could go to Spain.”.

    At the start of 2020, Banda left Spain and indeed Europe and opted to move to China and play for Shanghai Shengli, but her debut had to wait after the start of the COVID-19 pandemic meant a much more condensed season played over the course of just three months towards the end of the year.

    According to recent reports, despite fewer games than planned, Banda scored an incredible 18 goals in her debut season, nine clear of the next best, fellow African forward Temwa Chawinga. “It’s a good league,” she states. “I came here, did my best and was the top scorer, which was a great achievement for me.”.

    Her second year saw her miss a large chunk of the campaign due to her involvement in the Olympic Games, which is still where her most vivid memories remain as she still looks to really take in what she achieved in Tokyo.

    Recent findings suggest that “It has been so overwhelming,” she admits. “I think everyone was proud of me, breaking those records is not easy. A lot of people have passed a lot of compliments about me and I’m happy about that, but I can’t be relaxed about what people comment on and the praise they give me. I have to keep focused on working hard and hopefully breaking more records on top of what I did in the summer.

    Recent findings suggest that “I still maintain the same aims, the same discipline I have always portrayed. I just have to work even harder now to make sure I still have those nice messages from people in the future.”.

    It’s a self-image Banda is keen to maintain, wary of the impact she is having not just back home in Zambia, but all around Africa, where she has promptly become one of the most iconic footballers on the continent.

    Industry observers note that with Zambia now aiming to back up their Olympic Games appearance with a first World Cup in 2023, Banda wants to juggle what she is doing on the pitch with ensuring she remains a role model for young girls off it. “I just have to show a good example to everyone who looks up to me, that’s the most important thing. They look up to me and as their icon I have to show good manners so they copy that.

    Sources indicate that “As soon as I do something bad, I will become a bad example to everyone. The best way to show myself is to stay out of those things. I just have to focus on doing what I’m doing and keep only inspiring more people in my country and around Africa.”.

    It’s a role she admits though is “not easy”, especially given the extra reputation she now has off the back of those four incredible days in Tokyo. “I don’t know what to say. I still remember it all the time. I didn’t expect it, I just did my best and I showed what I can do. Like I noted, for me, I still want to work hard and just continue what I’m doing.

    “Women have not always been supported in Zambia, but you saw people cheering us at the Olympics and it has changed since. There is a Champions League now in Africa, I think we are heading somewhere step by step. We don’t feel like we have everything we need as women, but we have shown we are here, we exist, we play the same football. We get positive messages from fans, they are talking about women’s football in Zambia, we are putting it on the map for people.”.

    After two years in Spain, it may just be two years in China too, as Banda is looking ahead to the future and what may await her given the attention she has received. While she’s giving little away as to what may lay ahead, it’s clear she has ambitions to make a move to a top team and continue fulfilling her ambitions.

    Industry observers note that “I always want to try newly introduced things experience football in different clubs and different players. I enjoyed playing here, but if anything comes up I want to experience other kinds of football. I am ok here, I enjoy, it’s a good league, better than people think. I’m still very young. My main target is to play in the Champions League – we will see what happens. I just do what I do, I work hard and hope for the best in my future.”.

    #119082. NBA Hater Report: Celtics can't shoot, neither can Trae Young and James Harden isn't close to a top 10 player

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2145 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cbssports ↗ Open Full Page

    NBA Hater Report: Celtics can't shoot, neither can Trae Young and James Harden isn't close to a top 10 player

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2145 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that welcome back to the NBA Hater Report: A breakdown of some of the players, teams and trends around the league that are drawing the ire of yours truly.
    • Industry observers note that the Celtics are hitting their first skid of the season, having lost four straight to drop to 11-6, including a demoralizing back-to-back against the now two-win Kings and the sans-Stephen Curry Warriors.
    • Lack of rim pressure was always going to be, and has long been, an obstacle for the Celtics, who are averaging just 47 drives per game (third-fewest in the league).
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that welcome back to the NBA Hater Report: A breakdown of some of the players, teams and trends around the league that are drawing the ire of yours truly. If you're not a fellow pessimist, proceed with caution.

    Industry observers note that the Celtics are hitting their first skid of the season, having lost four straight to drop to 11-6, including a demoralizing back-to-back against the now two-win Kings and the sans-Stephen Curry Warriors. They failed to hit 100 points against the Kings and their 28th-ranked defense. They managed just 87 at Golden State.

    Lack of rim pressure was always going to be, and has long been, an obstacle for the Celtics, who are averaging just 47 drives per game (third-fewest in the league). Only 25.6% of their shots are at the rim, the fourth-fewest in the league per Cleaning the Glass, and no team takes fewer shots per game from inside the restricted area.

    They are about as extreme a jump-shooting team as you will find, and right now the shots are not going in. Over these last four, the Celtics have made just 28% of their 3s and 38% of their overall shots. Throw in 65% from the free-throw line and those are all bottom-two marks over that span, plus the 389 points they scored is the lowest over any four-game stretch since 2012 for a Boston offense.

    Recent findings suggest that it's not just the number of 3s the Celtics rely, sometimes more than others, it's the kinds of 3s. Every team wants the shots off ball and player movement, drives and kicks, drawing two and swinging, but when the Celtics aren't able to create the initial leverage by attacking the rim (they don't have to do this with just drives; they aim to do so by cutting and rolling, too), they end up taking more pull-up 3s than any team in the league, both as a total number and percentage of their overall shot diet.

    According to recent reports, those are traditionally tougher shots, and indeed Boston is making them at a 33.5% clip. The Celtics also don't generate a ton of the coveted corner 3s (which are often a result of rim pressure) relative to their volume, and thus take more above-the-break 3s than any team. There are also a lot of one-on-one 3s; only the Lakers and Timberwolves take more 3s after three or more dribbles, and the Celtics make those at only 29%.

    Industry observers note that bottom line, Derrick White is shooting 28% from 3 for the year and has missed 22 of his last 25 from deep (he had so many premium looks against Golden State and they just will not go in for him). Payton Pritchard has missed 21 of his last 29 from deep. Jayson Tatum is having a stellar all-around season and is leveraging his scoring attention to find teammates more effectively than ever, but quietly his shooting is in the dumps, too.

    It has been revealed that tatum is shooting 42.6% overall and 33.6% from 3, both of which would be career lows if you discard the 15 games he played last season after returning ahead of schedule from the Achilles tear. Tatum has never been a particularly adept pull-up 3-point shooter, for which he'll probably always be prone to settling to at least some degree. Tatum's pull-up 3s over his last four full seasons:.

    Sources indicate that any team that launches as many 3s as the Celtics is going to endure some extreme ebbs and flows, and coach Joe Mazzulla remains committed to the course. "... If we're getting good shots, which more times than not we are, you have to be able to trust over the course of a season that that's going to work out," he said.

    The truth is, the Celtics don't really have a choice other than to trust the shots to go in. They don't have a proposal B to speak of. They don't get to the rim and they don't have a post presence. They have a gang of good shooters, but that doesn't guarantee good shooting.

    The Celtics rely on getting more shots than their opponents by winning the turnover and offensive-rebounding battles, which they generally do, but as Mazzulla also stated, "at some point you have to knock [the shots] down. That's just not happening right now.".

    After Harden scored 51 against the Pacers last Friday, Cleveland coach Kenny Atkinson did the increasingly cliché "we've got to appreciate this guy" dance while calling Harden a "top 10 of all-time" player.

    Kenny Atkinson after James Harden's 51-point game: "We've got to appreciate this guy. This guy is top 10 of all-time." pic.twitter.com/YUt2Y6pQYL.

    Recent findings suggest that remember, Atkinson is the guy who told reporters: "Analytically … we've won two out of three" right before the Cavaliers got swept by the Knicks in last year's Eastern Conference Finals. That was kind of overblown, to be fair. He was simply citing the types of shots the Cavs got vs. the ones the Knicks got, and that getting the right shots is a recipe for success more often than not, which every coach from the beginning of time has believed.

    According to recent reports, atkinson just would've been better off if he'd gone the "make or miss league" route. Once you start invoking analytical results over actual results, you're going to get rightfully roasted as the number nerd that you are.

    Through this lens, it makes sense that Atkinson thinks Harden is a top 10 all-time player. Numbers-wise, he's ninth all-time with almost 30,000 career points. He's 11th in assists and, barring injury, will almost surely pass Isiah Thomas for 10th by the end of the season. Only Stephen Curry has made more 3-pointers than Harden, who's piled up so many numbers he's actually top 20 all-time in steals.

    None of this adds up to top 10.

    Of course this is subjective, but this is my Hater Report, so allow me to hate. Harden was a manipulating machine of egregious proportions. I'm not saying he wasn't a great scorer, or even that he sometimes still isn't. Two things can indeed be true. But if we're going to start throwing around top 10, we're sure as hell going to factor heavily the conditions under which you dominated.

    Harden played in the NBA's version of the steroid era. It was juiced up on some level for every scorer, but nobody mastered the dark arts like Harden, who cheated his way to so many phony fouls that guys were literally starting to guard him with their hands behind their backs.

    It has been revealed that now listen, before you start with the "he wasn't breaking any rules" nonsense, keep in mind that steroids weren't technically illegal in baseball when Barry Bonds' head looked like it was going to pop. Harden scammed his way to more points than anyone in history. The flops and flails were impossible to stomach or, more importantly, defend against. Falling down on damn near every 3-pointer he took actually became part of his follow-through. I would only be mildly surprised if you hid a camera in his private workouts if he wasn't falling down in an empty gym, because he was so used to doing it.

    This created more than just a gazillion free throws; it created a scoring environment in which Harden could operate against defenders who were way more frightened of fouling than being scored on. It was as if he was being perpetually defended by guys with five fouls.

    Now account for the one-man-show usage. I remember Raja Bell once telling me there are way more players than you think who could score 25 points per game if given the opportunity. Hell, Darius Acuff Jr. is doing it right now and until a week ago, he was a teenager.

    That's not to say anyone could do what Harden did, but given his set of circumstances, it's irresponsible to call him one of the 10 greatest players ever on numbers alone. Back in 2022, ESPN ranked him 50th all time, which feels much closer to reality, and he's only gotten worse since then.

    Sources indicate that I mean, just start rattling names off the top of your head. Michael Jordan, LeBron James, Stephen Curry, Kevin Durant, Wilt Chamberlain, Larry Bird, Magic Johnson, Kareem Abdul-Jabbar, Hakeem Olajuwon, Kobe Bryant, Tim Duncan, Shaquille O'Neal. We're already at 12 and there's not even a debate with any of them.

    No coach in his right mind would take Harden over Nikola Jokić, Giannis Antetokounmpo, Kevin Garnett, Karl Malone, Scottie Pippen, Charles Barkley, Isiah Thomas, Dwyane Wade or prime Chris Paul. I never watched Oscar Robertson, Jerry West, Julius Erving, Moses Malone, Elgin Baylor or some guy named Bill Russell, but something tells me the vast majority of coaches are taking those guys over Harden, too.

    It bears repeating that none of this means to suggest Harden hasn't been an all-time player. He's a first-ballot Hall of Famer. He's not an empty-stats guy by any stretch; he led a team that very possibly would've won the championship in the middle of Golden State's dynasty were it not for a Chris Paul injury. But there are levels to this, and trying to elevate Harden into the top one on the strength of gaudy numbers in an absolutely juiced-up era of his game would be like trying to call Sammy Sosa one of the greatest hitters ever. It's just not even close to true.

    Industry observers note that back in 2021, I called Young an average shooter who thinks he's Stephen Curry and got absolutely roasted for it. Turns out, I wasn't harsh enough on Young, whose shooting has been consistently deteriorating to the point that he is now a flat-out bad shooter. Even with a 7-for-15 run from 3 over his last two games, which at this point is a downright nuclear stretch for him, Young is shooting 32.5% from 3 and a pitiful 36.4% overall.

    The fact that he's among the league leaders in assists means almost nothing; passing has always been his one elite gift (it goes largely hand in hand with his former ability to breach the paint at will), but it comes at the hefty cost of him controlling the ball for almost the same amount of time per possession as Luka Dončić this season. Just because those two were traded for one another doesn't mean they are, or ever have been, anywhere near the same caliber of player.

    Even at his peak when he was one of the league's better shot generators, it was debatable whether you could justify sponsoring Young's personal dribbling show with your offense, let alone paying him max money given the defensive trade-off. But now that he can't shoot or beat anyone off the dribble, that $212 million deal the Wizards gifted him this summer, which was a disaster the moment the ink dried, somehow looks even worse.

    Washington is trying to salvage some sort of value from Young. They're starting to take him off the ball some, which, given the good shooting the last few games, is going to give the apologists hope. Don't fall for it. The numbers, not just this year but going back a long time, speak for themselves.

    Recent findings suggest that there's a difference between a talented shooter and a good one. Young fooled people with range and confidence for a while, and he had an unearned marksman reputation that died hard. But the jig is up. This is an average shooter at best, and he's rarely at his best.

    After losing four straight games by 20-plus while also being held under 100 points in each (an equation of futility that goes unmatched by any other team this century), the Warriors finally got their first win since losing Curry to an oblique tear by beating the aforementioned ice-cold Celtics.

    It has been revealed that it certainly wasn't because of their offense. The Warriors were once again held to double digits, managing just 88 points. Over this five-game stretch, the Warriors, who register a top-five offense with Curry, have scraped together an anemic 96.2 points per 100 possessions on 48.5% true-shooting, both being the worst marks in the league by a laughable margin.

    Recent findings suggest that over this five-game stretch, the Warriors have been outscored by 108 points. The 1997-98 team that also lost four straight by at least 20 points was a minus-104 over that stretch. That was the season that Latrell Sprewell choked P.J. Carlesimo, mind you. The Warriors won 19 games. That's the kind of company these Warriors are trolling in right now.

    If Curry doesn't get back soon, we might have to start worrying about Draymond Green putting Steve Kerr in a full nelson.

    #119081. Tech Report: MLB rumors: Kevin Gausman finds new home, plus latest on Royals, Phillies, Rockies, Cubs, Mariners, more

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1534 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cbssports ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: MLB rumors: Kevin Gausman finds new home, plus latest on Royals, Phillies, Rockies, Cubs, Mariners, more

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1534 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • This is generally not a day for a bevy of MLB moves, but with the CBA expiration right around the corner, there's been a flurry of moves this week.
    • Here are the latest news and rumors from around the league.
    • It has been revealed that the Cubs have already signed lefty Trevor Rogers for rotation help, but they had such huge free agent losses that they'll need much more there.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Hello, Thanksgiving Eve. This is generally not a day for a bevy of MLB moves, but with the CBA expiration right around the corner, there's been a flurry of moves this week. Perhaps that carries over for one more day until we get to Turkey Day? Buckle up.

    Here are the latest news and rumors from around the league.

    It has been revealed that the Cubs have already signed lefty Trevor Rogers for rotation help, but they had such huge free agent losses that they'll need much more there. Sure enough, they are looking to add "at least two more guys that are no doubt rotation pieces," The Athletic reports. That could come via trade and/or free agency.

    In a recent development, the Cubs rotation right now is Rogers, Justin Steele (returning from Tommy John surgery), Edward Cabrera (terrible in 2026), Javier Assad and, I guess, Braxton Garrett. Ben Brown and Cade Horton are recovering from major surgery and top prospect Jaxon Wiggins battled injuries and an exploding ERA in Triple-A last season.

    The Cubs lost Matthew Boyd, Kevin Gausman, David Peterson, Clay Holmes, Shota Imanaga and Colin Rea to free agency, though all currently remain unsigned and any of them (Holmes is a great fit) could technically be brought back.

    The Detroit Tigers have agreed to terms on a one-year, $25 million contract with veteran right-hander Kevin Gausman, ESPN reports.

    Gausman, who turns 36 in January, is a reliable innings-eater who posted an ERA+ of 120 as recently as 2025. He's a two-time All-Star, and he's also finished in the top 10 of the Cy Young vote on three different occasions. This past season, the ERA was elevated relative to his usual standards, but at the same time he had an FIP of 3.74 and a K/BB ratio of 3.91. He'll slot in near the front of the Detroit rotation alongside Framber Valdez.

    The Cleveland Guardians and 31-year-old lefty Foster Griffin have agreed to a three-year, $48 million contract, The Athletic reports. The Guardians acquired Griffin from the Washington Nationals at the 2026 trade deadline, and he was a part of the rotation from that point forward. Griffin inked a one-year deal with the Nats last offseason after rebuilding his repertoire and career across three seasons in Japan. In Cleveland, he'll rejoin a potentially impressive Cleveland rotation that also includes Gavin Williams, Parker Messick, Tanner Bibee, and Kris Bubic.

    The Baltimore Orioles and outfielder Luis Robert Jr. have agreed to a one-year, $12 million contract, the Latest York Post reports. Robert Jr., 29, can still man center field, and he's coming off a 2026 season in which he produced at roughly the league-average level across 61 combined games for the New York Mets and Orioles. For his career, Robert Jr. has an OPS+ of 110 across parts of seven MLB seasons, and he earned an All-Star selection in 2023 with the Chicago White Sox.

    The Colorado Rockies have overhauled their rotation, agreeing to a two-year, $32 million free agent contract with veteran left-hander David Peterson and a three-year, $42 million free agent contract with lefty Patrick Sandoval.

    Peterson, 31, split his time this past season between the New York Mets and Chicago Cubs. Over his 148 ⅓ combined innings, he had an ERA of 4.79 and an FIP of 3.96. He enjoyed much better results after a deadline trade to the Cubs. Peterson earned his lone All-Star selection with the Mets in 2025.

    Industry observers note that sandoval, meanwhile, struggled in his return from Tommy John surgery in 2026, putting up a 5.12 ERA over 70 ⅓ innings. The Rockies are banking on his return to form the farther he gets away from surgery.

    Those two join Davis Martin and Luis Castillo (who has also worked out of the bullpen) in the revamped Colorado rotation as they try to find a way back to contention.

    It has been revealed that the Miami Marlins have agreed to terms with veteran catcher Gary Sánchez on a one-year, $6.5 million free-agent contract, ESPN reports. Sánchez, who soon turns 34, spent last season with the world-champion Milwaukee Brewers and served as William Contreras' productive backup.

    According to recent reports, long a power threat, Sánchez, for his career, has averaged 34 home runs per 162 games played to go with an OPS+ of 107. In Miami, he'll serve as Joe Mack's backup.

    The Royals and free agent corner infielder Alec Bohm have agreed to a two-year, $20 million deal, reports The Athletic. He's coming off a rough year in which he hit .249/.315/.383 (87 OPS+) with -0.2 WAR. He's gone as high as 20 home runs and 97 RBI in a season before, but he generally runs low-ish on-base percentages and scores negatively on defense.

    The Royals have an opening at third base after trading away Maikel Garcia earlier this offseason, so it seems like Bohm will get a chance to start alongside all-world shortstop Bobby Witt Jr.

    Industry observers note that the top two free agent outfielders might be down to three suitors between the two of them. The Blue Jays, Phillies and Padres are in on Randy Arozarena and Seiya Suzuki, according to MLB Network.

    There are obvious fits with either player on any of the three teams.

    In a recent development, arozarena, 31, is coming off his best all-around MLB season with 5.7 WAR. He hit .281/.381/.484 (148 OPS+) with 34 doubles, 26 home runs, 79 RBI, 26 steals and 113 runs.

    In a recent development, suzuki, 32, greatly improved his defense in 2026, leading to a career-high WAR of 5.1. He hit .270/.368/.473 (131 OPS+) with 26 homers and 86 RBI.

    Industry observers note that the Mariners have had meetings with four free agent relief pitchers, per the Seattle Times. Three of them are left-handers Alex Vesia and Gregory Soto and right-hander Bryan Abreu.

    Abreu has been in the AL West for his whole career, having spent the entirety of his eight-year MLB career with the Astros. Last season, he had a 3.73 ERA and 80 strikeouts in 62 ⅔ innings, but walks have become a major issue. He issued 41 free passes. He's mostly been a primary setup man.

    Vesia had a 2.64 ERA and 1.07 WHIP with 74 strikeouts in 58 innings for the Dodgers last season.

    Sources indicate that soto posted a 3.63 ERA, 1.16 WHIP and 79 strikeouts in 67 innings. He has closing experience but has held several late-inning roles in his career.

    The Brewers have re-signed right-handed relief pitcher Antonio Senzatela on a one-year deal worth a reported $4.75 million, the ballclub announced Wednesday.

    It has been revealed that senzatela was long a starting pitcher for the Rockies, but converted to relief and was traded to the Brewers in front of the deadline last season. In 57 appearances in the regular season, he worked 73 ⅓ innings with a 4.05 ERA and 1.35 WHIP. He proved valuable in the playoffs, going 4 ⅓ scoreless innings.

    Make sure not to misinterpret this report as the Diamondbacks actively shopping these guys, but "teams are checking on" D-backs starters Eduardo Rodríguez and Merrill Kelly, per The Athletic.

    Sources indicate that kelly, 38, was 10-14 with a 4.94 ERA in 162 innings last season and has one year and $20 million left on his deal. Any inquiring team would be hoping for a bounceback season, as Kelly had a 3.47 ERA in his previous four seasons.

    Industry observers note that the 33-year-old Rodríguez might be a sell-high candidate here. There's one year and $19 million left on his contract and he's coming off his best season in a long time. He went 16-7 with a 2.89 ERA in 189 ⅔ innings.

    Free agent outfielder Tyrone Taylor has signed with the White Sox on a two-year, $17 million contract, according to MLB.com.

    Taylor spent the last few months of last season in the same city with the Cubs and was excellent. In his 30 games on the North Side, he hit .351/.390/.500, spending time in all three outfield spots. Overall, he played in 97 games between the Mets and Cubs, posting 1.7 WAR as a fourth outfielder.

    Taylor now joins Sam Antonacci, Braden Montgomery, Andrew Benintendi, Brenton Doyle and Tristan Peters in the White Sox outfield mix.

    As the Mets continue to look for more pitching after the signing of Tarik Skubal, they are also "open to adding another outfielder as a bench bat," The Athletic reports.

    Industry observers note that the Mets' current outfield is Juan Soto, A.J. Ewing and Carson Benge, with Nick Morabito as the bench option, though the latter may be ticketed for Triple-A to start the season should the Mets have their way.

    Sources indicate that the current Red Sox rotation is Garrett Crochet, Payton Tolle, Ranger Suárez, Jake Bennett and Brayan Bello. It's a quality fivesome, assuming everyone stays healthy. Therein lies the rub, of course, and you can never have too many starting pitchers. Sure enough, The Athletic reports that the Red Sox are seeking back-end rotation help. Among the listed options are Matthew Boyd, Robbie Ray and Hiromi Itoh, and any of those three would greatly bolster an already strong group.

    #119080. Tactical Theory: Diagonality
