    Latest Update: Lokomotive Leipzig, the 1987 Cup Winners’ Cup final and a rebirth from the ashes

    📅 25 Jan 2022 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1551 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thesefootballtimes

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A communist-era colossus of a stadium, the vast expanse of concrete stretching as far as the eye can see, enclosing a seething mass of humanity, congregating in their blue and yellow scarfs.
    • They have seen bigger crowds than this here, of course.
    • Industry observers note that football is the one thing that the authorities cannot control, the rebellious child of the model socialist state.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Picture the scene. A communist-era colossus of a stadium, the vast expanse of concrete stretching as far as the eye can see, enclosing a seething mass of humanity, congregating in their blue and yellow scarfs. They will need them tonight, for this open bowl is completely at the mercy of the elements. The fans do not care, however. This is the Zentralstadion in Leipzig and it is about to witness its finest hour.

    They have seen bigger crowds than this here, of course. The Turn-un Sportfest, the socialist government’s regular celebration of athletic achievement, can draw attendances of 100,000 or more. This is the largest crowd it will ever see for a football match, though – and that matters.

    Industry observers note that football is the one thing that the authorities cannot control, the rebellious child of the model socialist state. Football fans are not to be trusted; their first loyalty is to their teams and not to the party or the nation. They are prone to singing dissident songs and to bouts of hooliganism. Their unique culture is something that the state will never even try to understand. In these last years of the GDR, the terraces are also at the forefront of rebellion and change, operating, along with the church, as an open cover for opposition to one-party rule, hiding their protests in plain sight.

    It has been revealed that they will say there were 74,000 people inside the Zentralstadion that night, but many more will claim to have been there. It seems apparent to even the most casual observer that the real attendance is close to touching six figures. Later estimates put the actual number at 120,000.

    For the players who are about to step into this febrile atmosphere, this is their chance to make history. Lokomotive Leipzig are on the verge of reaching their maiden European final. They lead Bordeaux 1-0 from the first leg in France and now they stand 90 minutes away from the Cup Winners’ Cup final in Athens.

    In a recent development, lokomotive, the club, had already been through many incarnations. Their ancestors, VfB Leipzig, were the first national champions way back in 1903, when Germany was a unified nation. It is not apparent to those inside the ground tonight, but it soon will be again.

    Leipzig start the game with energy, flying into tackles, clearly fired up by the noise and passion of the crowd inside the stadium. It is Bordeaux, though, who take the early lead and go on to control the match.

    The home side continue to hold their own, however. They even have a chance to win the game late in the second half but Uwe Zotzsche’s penalty is saved by Dominique Dropsy in the Bordeaux goal. Extra-time is a tight affair and the match drifts to penalties.

    Leipzig goalkeeper René Müller saves from Phillipe Vercruysse but Lok’s joy is short-lived as Matthias Liebers promptly sees his kick saved by Dropsy. Both teams’ penalty taking is unerring from that moment on, taking the shootout to sudden death. The tension in the ground is unbearable as Zoran Vujović steps up with the score tied at 6-6. His earlier goal has taken the tie this far but now he looks gripped by nerves.

    In a recent development, he hesitates twice on his long run-up before scuffing his penalty straight at Müller. The Zentralstadion erupts: Lok are now one kick from glory. Incredibly, the man stepping forward to take the crucial penalty is none other than Müller himself, the goalkeeper who now has the chance to score the most crucial goal in his club’s history.

    Müller places the ball and starts his run with a determined look in his eyes before blasting his penalty high into the roof of the net. He wheels away, arms in the air, and is instantly mobbed in a sea of exultant teammates.

    There is something symbolic about the celebrations inside the stadium. The fans don’t know it but this is as good as it will get for GDR football. Within two years, protests will begin in this very city, as young people craving the freedom of expression of Western society crowd onto the streets that surround the Zentralstadion. These protests will spread all over the nation, culminating in the fall of the Berlin Wall on a cold November evening. Within four years, the GDR will be no more.

    Industry observers note that so what became of Lokomotive Leipzig and those men in yellow and blue shirts? The team itself would go on to lose the Cup Winners’ Cup final to a dynamic Ajax side containing Marco van Basten, Frank Rijkaard and a young Dennis Bergkamp.

    According to recent reports, in many ways Lokomotive’s fate since that April night in 1987 mirrors that of the former GDR. Desperate to throw off the negative associations of communism and to seem at one with their fresh western countrymen, the team ditched the name Lokomotive in 1991 to become VfB Leipzig once again. A brief foray into the Bundesliga followed three years later before the economic reality of eastern life in the united Germany bit hard. By 2004, the club that had stood on the brink of European glory a mere 17 years earlier had ceased to exist.

    Industry observers note that the old Zentralstadion was a ruin, housing a shiny new ground inside its crumbling bowl. The new stadium was used during the 2006 World Cup in Germany and is now the home of RB Leipzig, the controversial franchise club owned by the Austrian soft drinks giant Red Bull. As an image of capitalism’s utter triumph over communism, only the McDonalds that now stands on Checkpoint Charlie is more symbolic.

    It has been revealed that for many cities, this may have been the end of their famous old football club, but Leipzig is no ordinary place. The club’s fans rallied round and restarted Lokomotive Leipzig in the 11th tier of German football in time for the 2004/05 season. Fans rebuilt the club’s Bruno-Plache Arena brick by brick with their bare hands until it was fit to host football again.

    The response from the city was incredible. Lokomotive even broke the record for a lower-league football match in Germany when 12,421 spectators turned out for a game against Eintracht Grosbenden. The venue for this game? None other than the famous old Zentralstadion itself. The club that refused to die had come full circle.

    It would be painting an unnecessarily rose-tinted picture to pretend that everything has been plain sailing since then. Leipzig’s tendency to be a microcosm of the eastern half of Germany has continued as the years have progressed. Lokomotive have not been alone in battling neo-Nazi hooligan elements as the far-right has sought to exploit the economic troubles and resentment of the former GDR for its own ends.

    Industry observers note that the club has also failed to break out of the regional leagues despite plenty of near-misses over the last few years. However, the current picture is beginning to look altogether brighter. Leipzig is now an up-and-coming city, boasting a thriving tourism industry, trading in both shiny new architecture and GDR kitsch, or Ostalgia as it is called by locals.

    Lokomotive, too, are on the up. The club has made commendable efforts to drive out the hooligan element and to make the Bruno-Plache a more welcoming environment for everyone. They boast one of their most impressive squads in recent years and harbour real hopes of soon returning to the Bundesliga structure.

    Recent findings suggest that many lower league clubs have struggled to survive the empty stadiums, or “ghost games” as they are called in Germany, which have become a sad necessity of the COVID-19 pandemic. Lokomotive had their own unique solution to the problem. The club unveiled they would be selling tickets for €1 to a virtual game against the “invisible opponent” to raise money to pay the club’s 300 staff.

    The aim was to set a latest club attendance record, beating the 120,000 that were estimated to have been at the Zentralstadion for the Cup Winners’ Cup semi-final. Incredibly, Lok ended up selling 150,000 tickets for this imaginary game, the money keeping the club afloat through the months that followed. They do things differently in this unique city.

    According to recent reports, the joy of fans returning to stadiums this season has sadly been curtailed recently in the state of Saxony, where Leipzig resides, with matches temporarily being played behind closed doors once again. As a result, the Bruno-Plache Arena currently stands empty. Its last game with spectators was the derby against Chemie, another famous name from the GDR days. Lok won 1-0 in front of 6,000 passionate fans.

    According to recent reports, those fans may be absent at the moment but soon they will return to cheer on the men in yellow and blue shirts, for nothing can quell their devotion. To this day, they still tend to their beloved stadium, picking weeds out of its’ cracks and painting its seats. It might not quite be the Zentralstadion on that magical night in 1987, but Lokomotive Leipzig and their fans are home again. Who knows, they may have a few more glory nights left in them yet.

    By Billy Crawford @BillCrawford87.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    One of the best parts about Thanksgiving is reuniting with family, eating good food and watching sports. Whether it's watching a massive NFC North showdown on CBS between the Lions and Bears or tuning into one of the best college basketball games of the week between No. 11 Michigan State and Arkansas, Thanksgiving will have something for everybody.

    Michigan State star Jeremy Fears Jr. was named Preseason Player of the Year by CBS Sports and has looked the part through the first three weeks of the season. Fears, who is the No. 35 ranked player on CBS Sports Prospect Rankings for the 2027 NBA Draft, is also improving his draft stock ahead of a wide-open draft with his play.

    Industry observers note that if Fears is drafted in the first round this summer, he will join exclusive manufacturer with his brother Jeremiah Fears, who was selected No. 8 overall by the Pelicans in 2025. The Fears brothers could become the latest siblings to both get drafted in the first round of the NBA Draft if Jeremy is selected on the first day.

    Here is a list of siblings who were both drafted in the first round of the NBA Draft.

    Fears isn't the only notable sibling playing college basketball this season. Bryce James, the son of LeBron James, started the first three games of the season for Arizona. Kiyan Anthony, the son of NBA legend Carmelo Anthony, has been a key rotation piece for Syracuse this season. Andrej Stojaković, the son of one of the greatest shooters in NBA history (Peja Stojaković), has played like an All-American this season.

    Here are some of the most notable college basketball players playing this season with NBA bloodlines in their family.

    Basketball bloodline: Brother of Jeremiah Fears, who plays for the Pelicans.

    Recent findings suggest that the Fears brothers will have a chance to become the next set of brothers drafted in the first round of the NBA Draft. Jeremiah had a standout one-and-done season at Oklahoma before becoming a lottery pick. Jeremy redshirted during the 2023-24 season after being shot in the leg. Over the last three seasons, Jeremy has emerged as one of the best players in college basketball. He led the nation in assists last season and is on pace to do the same this season.

    Basketball bloodline: Son of Peja Stojaković, former NBA All-Star who played for Kings, Pacers, Hornets and Raptors from 1998-2011.

    It has been revealed that andrej has a completely different skill set than his father, who lit up the NBA in the 2000s as one of the best 3-point shooters in the sport. Andrej is off to an incredible start to the 2026-27 season, highlighted by a 46-point outburst against Duke, in which 12 of his 14 field-goal makes came from inside the arc. Andrej is playing like an All-American this season and is helping Illinois maintain a top-ranked offense without David Mirković in the lineup.

    Basketball bloodlines: Son of LeBron James, NBA's all-time leading scorer who currently plays for 76ers, brother of Bronny James, who plays for the Lakers.

    The son of one of the most famous athletes on the planet began the season as a starter for Arizona while coach Tommy Lloyd was trying to build his rotation in the midst of the RJ Godfrey eligibility dilemma. James does have bragging rights over his older brother and father because he was part of the Wildcats' Final Four roster last season, something no one in his family had done before.

    Basketball bloodline: Son of Gilbert Arenas, a three-time NBA All-Star during an NBA career that spanned from 2001-12 with the Warriors, Wizards, Magic and Grizzlies.

    After playing in 14 games last season, Arenas returned to USC for his sophomore season. It's looking like the right decision. Gilbert's son has developed into one of the best scorers in college basketball, averaging 21.3 points per game. Arenas has also boosted his draft stock tremendously and could be a lottery pick this summer.

    Basketball bloodline: Son of Carmelo Anthony, a Syracuse legend who played for Nuggets, Knicks, Thunder, Rockets, Trail Blazers and Lakers from 2003-2022.

    It has been revealed that after appearing in 29 games last season at his father's alma mater, Anthony decided to return to Syracuse for his sophomore season. Anthony is Syracuse's leading scorer (13.5 points per game) despite coming off the bench in all six games this season.

    Basketball bloodlines: Son of Carlos Boozer, who played for the Cavaliers, Jazz, Bulls and Lakers from 2002-15; brother of Cameron Boozer, a rookie for the Grizzlies after playing for the Blue Devils last season.

    With Cameron Boozer declaring for the NBA Draft, this season marked the first time Cayden didn't play on the same team as his brother. Boozer returned to Duke for his sophomore season instead of entering the transfer portal and has started five of his team's first six games this season and is averaging 6.2 points and 4.3 assists.

    Basketball bloodline: Son of Scottie Pippen, a Naismith Hall-of-Famer after his 17-season NBA career with the Bulls, Rockets and Trail Blazers.

    Pippen is at his third school in three seasons after previous stops at Michigan and Cal. In six games at Ohio State, Pippen is averaging 11.5 points, which ranks third on the team. He finished last season as Cal's second-leading scorer before entering the transfer portal.

    Basketball bloodlines: Son of Jason Richardson who played for the Warriors, Bobcats, Suns, Magic and 76ers in 14 seasons in NBA; brother of Jase Richardson, who plays for the Magic.

    Recent findings suggest that richardson, who was the No. 28-ranked recruit in the 2026 recruiting cycle by 247Sports, has appeared in four games this season for the Crimson Tide. Richardson started the Crimson Tide's season opener against Sam Houston State, where he finished with four points in 15 minutes.

    Basketball bloodline: Son of Andre Iguodala, a four-time NBA champion during his career with the 76ers, Nuggets, Warriors and Heat from 2004-23.

    Sources indicate that iguodala, who was a three-star recruit in the 2025 recruiting cycle by 247Sports, did not appear in a regular season game during his freshman year. However, the son of the former NBA Finals MVP has appeared in four games this season for the Bears.

    Basketball bloodline: Son of Trevor Ariza, an 18-year NBA veteran who won an NBA championship with the 2008-09 Lakers.

    Sources indicate that ariza, who was a four-star recruit in the 2026 recruiting cycle by 247Sports, is right now playing his freshman season at Oregon. Ariza has made four appearances off the bench and is averaging 5.0 points per game.

    Basketball bloodline: Brother of DaRon Holmes II, who presently plays for the Nuggets.

    Recent findings suggest that holmes, the No. 36 player in the 2026 recruiting cycle by 247Sports, is looking like a key rotational piece for the Wildcats. The brother of the former first-round pick out of Dayton has made six appearances off the bench this season for the No. 8 Wildcats.

    Basketball bloodline: Son of Dominique Wilkins, who is in the Naismith Hall of Fame after playing for the Hawks, Clippers, Celtics, Spurs during his long NBA career.

    According to recent reports, the son of one of the greatest dunkers in NBA history made 32 games off the bench for Georgia last season before transferring to play for the Golden Bears. He has started seven games this season for Cal.

    Basketball bloodline: Son of Jermaine O'Neal Sr., who played in NBA from 1996-2014 for the Trail Blazers, Pacers and several other teams.

    The son of the former six-time NBA All-Star is having a breakout season at SMU. After making 34 appearances last season, O'Neal has started all six of SMU's games this season and is averaging 12.3 points per game.

    Basketball bloodline: Son of Hakeem Olajuwon, a Naismith Hall-of-Famer after playing for the Rockets and Raptors from 1984-2002.

    In a recent development, the former four-star recruit has been a key piece for coach Kyle Smith this season. Olajuwon has appeared in six games (four starts) and is averaging 7 points per game. Notably, his younger brother, Malik Olajuwon, committed to and signed with SMU to play next season.

    Basketball bloodline: Son of Brandon Bass, who played in the NBA from 2005-17.

    Sources indicate that bass has made six appearances off the bench thus far during his freshman season at FSU. His best performance came in Florida State's first game, where he dropped 13 points against Florida A&M.

    Basketball bloodline: Son of Mo Williams, who played in NBA for 13 seasons, winning an NBA title with the Cavaliers in 2016.

    According to recent reports, williams is playing his freshman season at the same place where his father is an assistant coach. The former four-star recruit has been a key rotation piece for Mark Pope this season and is averaging 7.2 points off the bench.

    Basketball bloodline: Twin brother of Cooper Flagg, who was the No. 1 pick in the NBA Draft after playing for Duke.

    The twin brother of the No. 1 pick in the 2025 NBA Draft had to wait an extra year to play college basketball. That's because Cooper reclassified to join Duke in time for the 2024-25 season, while his brother played his senior season in high school. After making 32 appearances last season for Maine, mostly off the bench, Ace has started seven games for the Black Bears and is averaging 6.4 points.

    Basketball bloodline: Son of Penny Hardaway, a four-time All-Star during his 14-year NBA career.

    It has been revealed that the son of the current Memphis coach has had quite the college journey. He had two separate stints playing for his father at Memphis before transferring to Coastal Carolina this offseason. He has started one game this season at his new school.

    Basketball bloodline: Son of Brandon Roy, the Rookie of the Year in 2006-07 while playing for the Trail Blazers before his NBA career ended after a season with the Timberwolves in 2012-13.

    The son of the former Portland Trail Blazers star is in his second season at Washington. He has appeared in seven total games during his first two seasons at the college level.

    Basketball bloodline: Son of Richard Hamilton, who played for the Wizards, Pistons and Bulls from 1999-2013.

    The son of the former three-time NBA All-Star is in his freshman season at Oakland. He has six appearances off the bench this season.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, NFL halftime highlights have evolved since the beginning of the league. What began as marching bands and local high school bands has now turned into full productions.

    Thanksgiving has featured big performances from top artists since 1997, when Reba McEntire performed at the first Salvation Army Red Kettle Kickoff halftime show, which kicks off the Salvation Army's annual Red Kettle Campaign and encourages fans to give back to those in need.

    In a recent development, this year, three games will be played on Thanksgiving Day. Bears vs. Lions will be played at 1 p.m. ET on CBS and stream on Paramount+, Eagles vs. Cowboys will take place at 4:30 p.m. ET on FOX, and the Chiefs and Bills face off at 8:20 p.m. on NBC.

    It has been revealed that wu-Tang Clan will perform in Detroit, Miranda Lambert in Texas, and the Goo Goo Dolls in Latest York. This doesn't include the first-ever Thanksgiving Eve game between the Green Bay Packers and Los Angeles Rams, where U2 will perform at halftime.

    Here is a look at 10 of the most memorable Thanksgiving halftime show performances:.

    In a recent development, you can't mention Thanksgiving halftime reveals without mentioning Creed's Texas performance. There were silk aerial dancers, a man flying through with giant wings, mimes, choir singers and many other elements that left people with a lot of questions.

    Recent findings suggest that A 77-year-old Dolly Parton took the stage in a Dallas Cowgirl costume and proved why she is a country music legend. She performed "Jolene," "9 to 5" and made a medley with Queen's "We Will Rock You" and "We Are The Champions." Any Dolly performance is automatically iconic, and this was no different.

    Sources indicate that since she kicked off the tradition of Thanksgiving halftime highlights, McEntire has to make the list. She performed at Texas Stadium with a choir and dancers, along with the Cowboys cheerleaders. The country music legend performed on a star stage and wore Cowboys blue.

    Any Destiny's Child performance is automatically memorable. The Texas natives were an obvious choice for a Texas halftime show. The trio performed "Lose My Breath" and "Soldier" from their final studio album. A marching band and cheerleaders joined their performance.

    Mariah Carey may be the queen of Christmas, but she also knows how to put on a great Thanksgiving performance. The pop diva performed "Shake It Off" and "Don't Forget About Us" from her album The Emancipation of Mimi. The Ford Field performance also included a marching band and dancers. Carey began the performance being carried by men in football uniforms. People on the field created an "M" and "C.".

    Sources indicate that carrie Underwood has become an NFL staple, as the singer of Sunday Night Football's theme song. Her ties to the NFL also include a Thanksgiving halftime show performance. She sang her hit song "Before He Cheats" and "We're Young and Beautiful" in Texas, with an elaborate backdrop and silk aerial dancers.

    According to recent reports, sheryl Crow brought down the Texas house with her rock vibes on Thanksgiving Day. She performed "Good Is Good" and her biggest hit "If It Makes You Happy." With acrobatic dancers and ribbon twirlers, her exciting performance became an instant classic.

    In a recent development, the Jonas Brothers are one of the biggest boy bands of the early 2000s and 2010s, and their performance was a hit with any Disney Channel fans. The Jonas Brothers performed in 2008, singing hits including "Lovebug" and "Burnin Up." They became the first-ever repeat performers when they returned in 2022, singing new hits including "Only Human." Both performances were at the Cowboys' home.

    The American Idol winner and Texas native performed in front of the Cowboys' home fans. She performed "Walk Away," "Never Again," and "Since U Been Gone" in front of Dallas cheerleaders, pyrotechnics, and flashing lights.

    Jack White headlined last year's Lions Thanksgiving halftime show and surprised fans by bringing out Eminem. White opened with "That's How I'm Feeling" before introducing Eminem, who performed "Till I Collapse." The two Detroit natives were a hit with the Ford Field crowd.

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, the New York Knicks may have cut off contract extension talks with Karl-Anthony Towns before the season, but Towns is doing plenty of negotiating on his own behalf with his play.
    • In a recent development, towns leads the league with 13.9 rebounds per game.
    • Meanwhile, Towns is averaging 21.8 of just about the most efficient points possible for a shooting big man at 54% overall and 41.5% on five 3s a game.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, the New York Knicks may have cut off contract extension talks with Karl-Anthony Towns before the season, but Towns is doing plenty of negotiating on his own behalf with his play. Towns has been extraordinary for a Knicks team that still hasn't found its top form after winning the title, but is trending that way with five straight wins to get to 11-6.

    In a recent development, towns leads the league with 13.9 rebounds per game. It's not just his size; he is a technician on the glass with the way he gets into the body of his man to stop his forward momentum and then almost springs himself back toward the ball for a two-birds-with-one-stone maneuver.

    Meanwhile, Towns is averaging 21.8 of just about the most efficient points possible for a shooting big man at 54% overall and 41.5% on five 3s a game. His 15 straight double-doubles to start the season are a Knicks record. It's unlikely that he'll reach Bill Walton's all-time mark of 34 straight double-doubles to start the 1976-77 season, but with the way he's playing, you can't rule anything out.

    Towns now has 20 straight regular-season doubles dating back to last year, four times more than the next highest active streak (Victor Wembanyama right now has five straight). Towns gets to his 3s in every way. He pops. Stretches. His step-back is about the only thing not going for him at present, but it's a nasty weapon with how dangerous he is as a driver.

    It's tempting to think Towns should be firing off even more 3s, but he is so dialed in on his attack times and zones that it's best to just let him continue playing on balance. When Jalen Brunson is in, he steps back. When Brunson is out, he ramps up the scoring. He's become the best high-hub passer this side of Nikola Jokić; no dime is too ambitious for him, as he is into full anticipatory quarterbacking rather than waiting for things to show open, which marks the highest level of facilitation.

    Get it to Towns at the top and cut, and you've got a good chance for a bucket:.

    KAT continues to hoop, good cut from Landry pic.twitter.com/5FG2CAKkGg.

    KAT with the beautiful assist to Josh Hart for an easy 2.Can you imagine how fun playing basketball with KAT must be? pic.twitter.com/5L9QwYR2N8.

    Watch here as the Knicks flank Towns with a pair of two-man screening actions on each side. The first one, on his right, doesn't yield anything. But like a quarterback, he keeps going through his progressions until a second source produces fruit.

    These cuts are open for the Knicks because Towns, first, has pulled the massive man away from the basket, and even more when Brunson is on the court and the defense has to be so concerned with the two-man handoffs that the lid is completely lifted.

    Alexander Isak starts to justify £125m price tag with double

    📅 04 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 26 min read (5270 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that there was a centre-forward who played for Newcastle a couple of years ago.
    • Everyone wanted him, but Liverpool signed him for £125m in August 2025.
    • If you had wondered what had happened to him, he reappeared at Portman Road.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that there was a centre-forward who played for Newcastle a couple of years ago. Do you remember him? He was as quick as greased lightning, played on his instincts, had a shot like cannon and could come up with a finish for every situation.

    Everyone wanted him, but Liverpool signed him for £125m in August 2025. His name was Alexander Isak but shortly after arriving on Merseyside, it was like he went missing, as the guy who played in red last season bore only a physical resemblance to the guy who had played in black-and-white.

    If you had wondered what had happened to him, he reappeared at Portman Road. They say good things come to those who wait. Although nobody at Liverpool would have expected such a delay to see the real Isak, there were no complaints that his career at the club has finally taken off.

    Taking the headlines from Bradley Barcola on a massive night at Portman Road was going to take some doing, but Isak did just that with a double salvo in the opening nine minutes, a flurry so potent it was like a boxer charging out of their corner and seeing the first blows land flush on their opponent’s jaw.

    Sources indicate that poor Ipswich. There is universal recognition that Liverpool are a team – and a club – in transition but they had four players in Isak, Florian Wirtz, Cody Gakpo and Victor Muñoz who had the potential to dismantle the hosts if they clicked and that is precisely what happened.

    “With Alex, it is clear,” remarked Andoni Iraola. “If he is fit, if he is available, if he is in a good shape, he will produce the numbers. My demand with Alex will not be about the goals. It will be about other things so we can play well. And if we play well, we are in good positions. Then goals will come.”.

    So for all the noisy backing they received from the stands and for all the effort Gary O’Neil’s side put into a contest that TV companies had chosen to broadcast because there was a potential for drama, Isak blew a hole in Ipswich’s hull in the sixth minute and they were submerging from there on in.

    A blistering finish from Alexander Isak! 💥 pic.twitter.com/jSGlIZsQtA.

    How Isak, who had scored against Nottingham Forest last weekend, needed a night like this when he made a genuine difference. But the same was true, too, for Iraola. We live in an era where someone has to be in the eye of a storm and the Basque will know what comes with his upcoming territory.

    It had clearly irritated Iraola that Liverpool had gone behind four times in their opening two fixtures and during his pre-match media briefing, he effectively gave a sermon at one point on how slow starts, or giving the opposition a helping hand, would no longer be tolerated.

    Recent findings suggest that quietly, Iraola is making his presence felt. The task he faces is significantly different than the one O’Neil is accomplishing – keeping Ipswich in the division against the odds – but Liverpool’s head coach is a man who knows his own mind and is not afraid to make decisions.

    He had responded to criticism of his midfield at Newcastle on the opening weekend by dropping Ryan Gravenberch for the fixture with Forest and his response to scrutiny about his right-back seven days ago was to drop Jeremie Frimpong and bring in Ronald Araújo.

    Industry observers note that iraola certainly picked the right team: Araújo, the loan capture from Barcelona, added stature to the back four and there was harmony in how they moved. The Uruguayan’s first instinct was to stay back and Liverpool looked better for it, even if O’Neil, incredibly, felt Ipswich had the better of things.

    Emersonn, Ipswich’s Brazilian striker, did not see the ball in the opening exchanges and, by the time he did, Liverpool had zoomed into the distance to such an extent that you felt it was going to be impossible for them to peg their visitors back.

    “I hate having to talk about good performances when you do not get points,” O’Neil declared to a room full of raised eyebrows and you can only assume his message was to ensure that morale in the dressing room was not drooping.

    What damage was inflicted with Liverpool’s first significant attack. Gakpo, the subject of an £80m bid from Manchester City, was never going to allow transfer speculation to disrupt his focus and he nudged a perfect little ball into Isak’s path in the sixth minute to show his wellbeing.

    The next move confirmed the return of Isak. One touch gave him an avenue to shoot, the next was a shot with his right foot that was so hard from 16 yards, on an angle, it bent the wrists of Kjell Scherpen as it howled into the net. Critics will feel Ipswich’s keeper should have done better.

    Industry observers note that your first thought was to think of the first goal Isak scored in English football in September 2022, a similarly venomous drive, against Liverpool at Anfield. He oozed quality that evening, his pace and skill had Jürgen Klopp’s defenders persistently fretting and this is what he was doing again.

    According to recent reports, it was no coincidence that three minutes later, he came up with another wonderful goal. This one owed much to the beautiful pass Gakpo presented to him, an inch-perfect through ball with the outside of his right foot, but Isak still showed great poise to bamboozle Scherpen.

    Inside NINE minutes Alexander Isak has two goals! ⚡️ pic.twitter.com/3UGq0bwqRm.

    “He owes me a few assists now!” chirped the selfless Gakpo.

    A hat-trick could have arrived in the 32nd minute but Isak was a kneecap offside as he dispatched a pass from Wirtz and, perhaps, he will have been disappointed to have made way on the hour having not secured the match ball for his efforts.

    Liverpool, too, will be frustrated that they did not made sure of three points before the time Isak made way for Barcola – what Alexis Mac Alliser was thinking when he fluffed an unmarked header from six yards, only he will know – but it was not a night to nitpick.

    In a recent development, there will be easier assignments on the horizon for Ipswich, even though O’Neil insisted they more than held their own against world-class opponents. And you can say for sure there will be more goals and wins for Liverpool and Isak if they continue in this encouraging manner.

    It has been revealed that “I witnessed what a great coach he was at Bournemouth. He is not the sort of manager you are going to see making clever patterns in his box. He just does not see the risk. He will want to get the ball to the players who want to make a difference. Coaches do not show how good they are by how they play out from the back. The important thing is when you get it in the final third, you make things happen. That is what he will want to improve. He will want Alexander Isak when he has not got the ball to press. He will want the same of Florian Wirtz. The difficulty will come with Champions League football and not putting too many demands on his players. If he gets it right, he has got a wonderful squad to work with.”.

    "My demands will not be about the goals, my fights with him are about other stuff." Andoni Iraola speaking about Alexander Isak 🔊 pic.twitter.com/B4zUG2IGfS.

    It has been revealed that “He has had good minutes, a good pass in a counter, a good couple of chances when he was going against the goalkeeper and we have not found him. We need to learn these movements because he will be there threatening in behind all the team. But he looks confident on the ball as always. He had not played any competitive minutes since the World Cup so we had to be a little bit more careful.”.

    "Yeah, that's nice" 😁Alexander Isak talks through his second goal vs Ipswich 🔍 pic.twitter.com/diG2xv50Bw.

    Industry observers note that we are about to find out the two starting XIs at Portman Road. Will Bradley Barcola start for Liverpool on his debut?

    The third matchday of the new Premier League season kicks off at Portman Road as newly-promoted Ipswich host Liverpool.

    Andoni Iraola has drawn his first two games in charge of Liverpool, both 2-2 stalemates against Newcastle and Nottingham Forest respectively. Liverpool secured a move for forward Bradley Barcola from PSG in the final few days on the window for a fee that could rise to £123m and the Frenchman is set to make his Liverpool debut tonight.

    It has been revealed that “We are very happy with Bradley,” Iraola stated. “He was our priority; to sign a very good player in that position. He has come with the right mentality. I like that he wanted Liverpool a lot, he just wanted to come here. That is a good first sign. Being the player he is and the things he has won recently, he has come with the willingness to help us. I am very happy with him.

    Recent findings suggest that “He trained well with us, and if everything goes well in today’s [Thursday] training, he will definitely be available for tomorrow [tonight]. He has trained with us three times. He has not had minutes in pre-season but he has been training normally with the group. It is a decision we have to make. We have to consider that he has not had minutes in pre-season.”.

    Liverpool won both fixtures when Ipswich were last in the Premier League two seasons ago, including a 2-0 win on the opening weekend in Arne Slot’s first game in charge of Liverpool as they went on to win the Premier League that season.

    It has been revealed that ipswich won their first home game on their return to the Premier League, beating Sunderland 2-1 on the opening weekend. However, they fell to a 5-2 defeat in their first away game at Manchester United. Over the course of the summer transfer window, Ipswich made a total of 14 signings and spent over £200m.

    It has been revealed that “What we can do is perform in a way that always gives us a real chance, which we have done so far,” Ipswich boss Gary O’Neil remarked. “We were in that game at Manchester United until a couple of moments took it away from us. We were in it, so that is what we need to do, we need to make sure that no matter who it is, whether it is Liverpool, Manchester United, Manchester City, when they come to Portman Road, we need to make sure we are right in the game to give ourselves opportunities. We will always be a threat; we have scored four goals in two games. That is really good for a promoted side. We look a goal threat, and we need to keep that going and that will be tested.”.

    Team news from Portman Road to follow shortly.

    Edmundo: O Animal

    📅 06 Feb 2022 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2375 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thesefootballtimes

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that originally featured in the sold-out Brazil magazine, support high-quality, wholly independent journalism by ordering our magazine.
    • A cauldron full of seething excitations: that’s how Sigmund Freud describes the id, the psychological structure responsible for our base desires.
    • Industry observers note that his legend, like so many others of Brazilian football, began in the exacting slums of Rio de Janeiro.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that originally featured in the sold-out Brazil magazine, support high-quality, wholly independent journalism by ordering our magazine. It’s what keeps everything online free.

    A cauldron full of seething excitations: that’s how Sigmund Freud describes the id, the psychological structure responsible for our base desires. The id, Freud argues, must be kept in check to prevent man from acting impulsively against his own interests. A failure to repel one’s instincts, he warns, can have devastating consequences, not only for man but also his contemporaries. Nobody in football knows this more than Edmundo.

    Industry observers note that his legend, like so many others of Brazilian football, began in the exacting slums of Rio de Janeiro. Teixeira de Freitas Street may be just 30km from Ipanema, but for the downtrodden inhabitants of Niterói, it may as well be 3,000.

    Recent findings suggest that whilst the Maracanã glistened across Guanabara Bay, Reinaldo de Souza was trying to raise a family. A barber like his father and brother before him, he struggled to make ends meet whilst his wife worked long hours as a cleaner. With nothing to distract them from the long period without their parents, brothers Edmundo and Luizinho passed their time like any other child in their street. Football became their home, and the pickup games on the beach became their education.

    Industry observers note that it was just as well for Edmundo, who indicated no interest in academia. “Dinho”, as he was known to his family and friends, was focussed on one thing and one thing only. Even at a young age his talent was evident, a diminutive dribbler with a charring swagger, whose talent with the ball was matched only by the sharpness of his temper. He knew he was good and he wasn’t shy about it.

    Sources indicate that it was his aunt who first spotted his talent. Maria had taken to minding the boys whilst their parents worked, and she would ferry Edmundo to practice and back as well as into the city to watch his beloved Vasco. It wouldn’t be long, though, before he graduated from fan to the first team. Aged 15, Edmundo was invited to trial with Botafogo’s youth wing. Fogão coach Tinoco knew genius when he saw it, and the youngster left Teixeira de Freitas behind for the major time.

    It’s at this point in the story where the prodigy defies the odds to succeed. But Edmundo’s tale isn’t one of romance or glamour, and it was at Botafogo that his nascent talent for self-destruction first became evident. With Maria struggling to afford the transport to and from the Botafogo facilities, Edmundo moved into the club’s youth lodging, but barely after joining he was expelled for walking naked through the grounds.

    According to recent reports, luckily, Vasco didn’t mind exhibitionists. Perhaps they were swayed by an astonishing goal Edmundo had scored in a youth game in August 1991, where he had slalomed past an entire defence and goalkeeper before depositing a casual finish into an unguarded net.

    It has been revealed that after impressing for the reserves, Vasco coach Nelsinho gave him his debut in January 1992. The result, a 4-1 rout against Corinthians, augured well for a season in which the Vazcaínos would win the Carioca State Championship. Edmundo had been a revelation, dovetailing superbly with the mercurial Bebeto as his side finished third in the Brasileirão, but his strong personality led to continued clashes with his teammates.

    Sources indicate that the previous 17 years had been a disaster for Palmeiras fans. They had watched on trophyless as Corinthians and São Paulo won their first national and international titles respectively. In 1992, however, they would be rescued by the investment of the multinational conglomerate Parmalat.

    In a recent development, with Verdão surging thanks to Italian capital, coach Vanderlei Luxemburgo set about building one of the finest teams in Brazilian football history. Roberto Carlos, César Sampaio and Rivaldo were bright-eyed wunderkinds, but it was the capture of Edmundo for a record fee of $2m that captured fans’ imaginations. Vasco president Eurico Miranda was less than magnanimous, suggesting he was glad to get rid of a player who had been “a problem” for the dressing room.

    According to recent reports, nevertheless, Edmundo would lead his upcoming side to two straight Brasileirão titles and a State Championship. But “O Animal”, as he was christened by commentator Osmar Santos, once again found time to marry triumph with treachery. On 30 October 1994, São Paulo hosted Palmeiras at the Morumbi.

    According to recent reports, like any Paulistano derby, it was a hot-blooded encounter, but both sides were resigned to a draw as the minutes ticked down. That was before Edmundo was on the receiving end of a particularly dodgy tackle near the touchline. Incensed, he raged at São Paulo coach Telê Santana on the bench, before seeking his retribution against striker Euller moments later.

    In a recent development, A scrum ensued, with Edmundo punching André Luiz and slapping Juninho Paulista, prompting a full-scale fight between the teams in the process. By the time his teammate Antônio Carlos dragged him into the tunnel, six players had been sent off. Edmundo scored both his side’s goals that day, but nobody remembers them.

    It wasn’t the only sour note. The year before, he had been given a 40-day suspension for pushing a referee in the face, whilst he also found time to get into a fistfight with Antônio Carlos, the very man who had rescued him from the ravenous São Paulo players. Repeated fallouts with Luxembergo, meanwhile, were par for the course. Five red cards in one season spoke of a man seemingly incapable of self-restraint.

    Industry observers note that in 1995, he would even be detained by Ecuadorian police, his frustration at missing a penalty in the Copa Libertadores causing him to kick out at a local cameraman. It was only with the intervention of the Brazilian government that his release from the country was negotiated.

    In a recent development, despite winning everything with Palmeiras, the allure of Rio always held sway for Edmundo. In 1995, he joined a club that boasted 15 per cent of the country’s population as fans. Flamengo wanted to build an “attack of dreams”, with Dinho starting alongside Romário and Sávio as the club set their sights on continental domination.

    Unfortunately they didn’t know how to defend, a leaky defence and problems off the field scuppering their chances. A terrible year was summed up in the most brutal of fashions when, during the 1995 Supercopa Sudamericana against Vélez Sarsfield, Edmundo was knocked out cold by a vicious punch from Flavio Zandoná. Except for Palmeiras fans, hardly anybody was sympathetic.

    Off the field, Edmundo had endured a nightmare, but on 2 December 1995, his life descended into hell. After partying in a nightclub during the carnival, an inebriated Edmundo got into his Jeep Cherokee before driving straight into a Fiat Uno in the Lagoa suburb of Rio. The car, which had been travelling at 60mph in a 40mph zone, careened straight into a telephone pole. All three passengers died from their injuries.

    Industry observers note that A tearful Edmundo was charged with involuntary manslaughter, whilst Flamengo tore up his contract. Not only did he face a possible jail sentence, but he also found himself without the one thing that had been constant in his life: football.

    It would be Corinthians who offered him hope just 45 days later. As Edmundo’s lawyers interceded on his behalf, his attempts to concentrate on football hit an immediate snag, with the striker walking out on the club before he had made a single appearance. Eurico Miranda, the man who had greeted his departure from Vasco with such disdain years earlier, successfully sought to bring him back home.

    Sources indicate that it was the best season of Edmundo’s career, as he broke the Brazilian scoring record with 29 strikes. His form was so impressive that some argued for his inclusion as a starter over Ronaldo for the 1998 World Cup, but coach Mário Zagallo resisted, citing his disruptive influence on the squad.

    Recent findings suggest that despite a last-minute change of heart that saw him included in the final selection, Zagallo would be proven right. Edmundo would spend the entire tournament complaining about a lack of minutes, even contacting a Rio radio station to air his frustration publicly. When Ronaldo suffered a seizure before the final in Paris, Edmundo seemed to have finally been given his chance, only for the young superstar to emerge for the game amidst accusations of cover-ups and veiled suggestions of conspiracy.

    According to recent reports, no matter. His 38 goals in 44 games had piqued Fiorentina owner Vittorio Cecchi Gori’s attention, and Edmundo was brought to Florence to augment one of Serie A’s most fearsome attacks. Alongside Rui Costa and Gabriel Batistuta, Edmundo would be charged with bringing domestic and European glory to La Viola. More importantly, though, it was a fresh start a thousand miles away from the flashbulbs and straplines of his home country.

    Things went well at first, with the Brazilian combining lethally with Batistuta to fire his club to the top of Serie A. By the time Milan visited the Artemio Franchi in February, the home side had a chance to cement their lead, before Batistuta collapsed to the turf with an injury that would rule him out for two months.

    It has been revealed that any normal footballer would have assumed the goalscoring mantle. Any footballer except for Edmundo would have been focused on delivering his team’s first Scudetto in 30 years. The Brazilian, however, was nowhere to be seen, having exercised a clause in his contract that allowed him to attend the Rio carnival back home.

    Recent findings suggest that batistuta, like most of his teammates and the supporters, was incensed. “He was the right man if anyone wanted to have fun,” admitted the Argentine. “But to win something, he was not right.” By the time Edmundo returned to the club, his strikerless teammates had surrendered their lead, and would finish 14 points behind Lazio in third.

    It has been revealed that in each of his 18 months on the peninsula, Edmundo had made clear his desire to return home. When Eurico Miranda and Vasco called for him a third time, the transfer was as good as done. Back at his boyhood club and with the love of the fans behind him, Edmundo regained something close to his best form. The arrival at the club of Romário six months before the 2000 World Club Championship, however, reopened old wounds.

    The pair had been friends until 1998, before falling out after Romário’s beach bar in Rio was found to contain a derisory painting of Edmundo on one of the bathrooms stalls. When Romário refused to take it down, the pair fell out in spectacular fashion, so much so that when he joined Vasco, their relationship became a massive media circus. Their feud has been covered in excruciating detail in Brazil and beyond; suffice to say, these two giant talents and their commensurate egos found cohabitation difficult.

    It has been revealed that even the intercession of Vasco’s own priest, Padre Lino, couldn’t resolve their differences – not that Sir Alex Ferguson would have noticed. Romário and Edmundo combined with brutal efficiency to annihilate Manchester United in January 2000. After setting up Baixinho for the first, Edmundo had watched his partner capitalise on a second Gary Neville error to put the Brazilians two goals up.

    Recent findings suggest that on 43 minutes, Edmundo joined in himself, scoring a goal that summed up everything about what made him a special, irascible talent. Receiving an innocuous ball from Gilberto on the edge of the box, Vasco’s number 7 spun Mikaël Silvestre with the outside of his right boot, before sliding a finish past a hapless Mark Bosnich.

    Recent findings suggest that it was a moment of pure relief. Three months earlier, Edmundo had been strongly criticised by animal rights campaigners, after he was pictured giving beer and whiskey to a chimpanzee at his son’s first birthday party. He’d also spent a night in jail as a result of his ongoing trial, before his lawyers intervened to appeal. If he was trying to stay out of the headlines he was doing a very bad job of it, but the goal against United ensured he would finally be making waves for the right reason. It proved to be a brief respite.

    The “worst moment” of Edmundo’s career would arrive in the final of the same tournament, his missed penalty consigning Vasco to the runners-up medal at the hands of Corinthians. It was his last meaningful contribution at the highest level.

    Brief but tumultuous spells at eight clubs – including a further two stints at Vasco and another at Palmeiras – followed, but Edmundo failed to recapture the violent genius that had been his unmistakable trademark.

    More tragedy would befall him in 2002, when his brother was found murdered in the back of his car in Rio. By the time the body was found, it was already in an advanced state of decomposition. Edmundo, overcome with grief, couldn’t bear to attend the funeral.

    In 2011, the shadow that had hung over Edmundo’s life for 16 years was lifted. Magistrate Joaquim Barbosa ruled that, in the case of the fatal car crash that had claimed three lives, the statute of limitations had expired. Edmundo was free, but the grief of the moment still lives with him every day. “I am an eternal repentant,” he admitted in an interview with Brazilian media. “This sadness does not pass.”.

    There is no doubt that Edmundo’s career, with its litany of violent indiscretions and scurrilous headlines, makes less than pretty reading. But is he really, as one Brazilian journalist put it, “a liability to mankind”, or is he simply a deeply flawed human being, a man who struggled to reconcile a blessed gift with a cursed temperament? It’s a question that foregoes a simple answer. But what is simple is that Edmundo Alves de Souza Neto remains one of his country’s greatest talents. On the pitch at least, he is unassailable.
